description_full: Associated Banc-Corp, a bank holding company, provides various banking and nonbanking products and services to individuals and businesses in Wisconsin, Illinois, Missouri, Texas, and Minnesota. It offers lending solutions, including commercial loans and lines of credit, commercial real estate financing, construction loans, letters of credit, leasing, asset-based lending and equipment finance, loan syndications products, residential mortgages, home equity loans and lines of credit, personal and installment loans, auto finance and business loans, and business lines of credit. The company also provides deposit and cash management solutions, such as commercial checking and interest-bearing deposit products, cash vault and night depository services, liquidity solutions, payables and receivables solutions, and information services; specialized financial services comprising interest rate risk management and foreign exchange solutions; fiduciary services consisting of administration of pension, profit-sharing and other employee benefit plans, fiduciary and corporate agency services, and institutional asset management services; and investable funds solutions, including savings, money market deposit accounts, IRA accounts, CDs, fixed and variable annuities, full-service, discount, and online investment brokerage; investment advisory services; and trust and investment management accounts. In addition, it offers deposit and transactional solutions, including checking, credit and debit cards, online banking and bill pay, and money transfer services. The company operates loan production offices in Indiana, Kansas, Michigan, New York, Ohio, and Texas. Associated Banc-Corp was founded in 1861 and is headquartered in Green Bay, Wisconsin.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 4K people. Revenue per employee of $356K ranks in the below the sector median among Financial Services peers. Each employee generates $139K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $2K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 10× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: Associated Banc-Corp is a mid-cap financial services business with a $5.6B market cap on $1.5B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +2.9pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $579M in free cash flow — roughly 39 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.30× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.1× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 0.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 13% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.3) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are overwhelmingly selling (100% sell ratio) — the people who know the business want less of it
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

sect: Its 39% operating margin runs 10pp above the Financial Services median (29%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.50x).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 19% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 23% and a beta of 0.91, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.41 vs 5y 0.89), so read it loosely.
About $54.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 50% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 62% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 36% below its DCF fair value of $47.39, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 23%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $36.68 to $62.01 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Financial Services peers: P/FCF 9.7 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 22% above its 10-year median.
The 10 covering analysts target $34.50 on average, 14% above the price.
The price implies 0.8% annual cash-flow growth, 7pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.51).
It converts 39% of revenue into free cash flow.
As a lender it runs a net interest margin of 3.12% and an efficiency ratio of 58%.
It earns a 10% return on equity.
Operating margin is running 9pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: CET1 capital of 10.2% sits comfortably above the ~7% regulatory minimum with buffer.
Non-performing loans are 0.42% of the book, a clean credit profile.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.3% over 3 years, 3.1% over 5 years and 4.0% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Analysts expect 11.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 12.7%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 83%.
It returns 2.8% a year to shareholders (3.3% in dividends).
The share count has grown 4.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 40 consecutive years, raising it 6.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 4,173 employees, each generates about $356K of revenue, 0.7x the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 2.8% a year.
That works out to $139K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.5M (10x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).

profile.head: Watch: no strong case either way.
